page18_img_1.png.title: Box plots of generic method vs type declaration counts across projects
page18_img_1.png.description: Horizontal box plots compare the per-project counts of generic method declarations (top row) and generic type declarations (bottom row). The x‑axis is logarithmic (ticks at 1, 10, 100, 1000), and the median and interquartile ranges show that user-defined generic types are generally more numerous than generic methods (the paper reports an almost 2:1 ratio). The type-declaration distribution has a longer right tail and larger whiskers, indicating greater variability and some projects with very high counts, while methods are clustered at lower counts across most projects.

page17_img_2.png.title: Squirrel‑SQL annotation names and frequencies
page17_img_2.png.description: Two-column table from Squirrel‑SQL listing annotation identifiers (left) and their occurrence counts (right). The most frequent annotations are Override (1,935), Test (636), and Before (274), followed by SuppressWarnings (196) and After (158). Less common entries include Ignore (16), GUITest (4), Deprecated (3) and several annotations with 2 occurrences (TestExecutionListeners, RunWith, ContextConfiguration). The values indicate heavy use of standard and testing-related annotations in this project, with few project-specific annotations.

page17_img_1.png.title: Top parameterized generic types in Squirrel‑SQL (counts)
page17_img_1.png.description: A ranked list of the most frequent parameterized types in the Squirrel‑SQL codebase with occurrence counts. The top three are List<String> (351), ArrayList<String> (221), and HashMap<String,String> (157), showing a strong bias toward collections of String. Other frequent entries include List<ITableInfo> (96), Class<?> (91), Collection<String[]> (77), and several project-specific or array parameterizations (e.g., List<ArtifactStatus> 61, Vector<String> 58, List<Object[]> 33). Overall the table highlights that standard collection types (especially Lists and Maps parameterized with String) dominate generic usage in this project.

page14_img_1.png.title: Raw, generic, and annotation counts across 20 established Java projects
page14_img_1.png.description: Stacked bars show, for each of 20 established open-source Java projects, the total counts (in thousands) of raw types (red), parameterized/generic types (blue), and annotations (green). Eclipse.jdt has by far the largest total (roughly 16–18k combined), dominated by raw types with smaller portions of generics and annotations, while projects like Azureus and Spring are also large. JEdit and Squirrel‑SQL stand out for relatively large blue segments (generics), and FindBugs and Spring show noticeable green annotation usage. The chart visualizes the paper’s observation that many established projects still use more raw types than parameterized types and that a few projects account for most annotation and generic usage.

page19_img_1.png.title: Unique parameterizations per user-defined generic type (established vs recent projects)
page19_img_1.png.description: Two horizontal box plots (y: established, recent) show the distribution of the number of distinct type arguments used to instantiate each user-defined generic class; the x-axis is the number of unique parameterizations on a log scale (ticks at ~1, 10, 100). Established projects are tightly skewed toward small counts (38% of generic classes were instantiated with exactly one type, 80% had fewer than five; mean ≈ 4.8), while recent projects have a similar lower portion but a longer right tail (23% single-parameter, 76% under five, mean ≈ 7.5) with several extreme outliers (points) reaching many dozens to ~100 parameterizations. The figure emphasizes the positive skew in both groups and that most user-defined generics are instantiated with only a handful of distinct type arguments, with a few classes accounting for large numbers of parameterizations.

page39_img_1.png.title: Contributors' annotation introductions/removals over time (established projects)
page39_img_1.png.description: A 4x5 grid of small time-series plots (one per established project) showing annotation introductions/removals on the y-axis versus date on the x-axis. Each subplot plots the top contributors (different colored lines with a legend) and visualizes how many annotations each contributor added or removed over time: many projects show a single contributor with large, stepped increases (for example FindBugs, Commons‑Collections, JEdit, Squirrel‑SQL, Hibernate, Lucene, Maven, and Spring), while others show near-zero activity (Ant, Jetty, Log4j, Xerces). The sharp vertical jumps in several plots indicate abrupt bursts of hundreds or thousands of annotations (consistent with the paper’s observation of large, likely automated commits), supporting the paper’s finding that annotation adoption is typically driven by one or two “champion” contributors rather than evenly by the community.

page10_img_1.png.title: Established Java projects: developers, age, dates, and LOC
page10_img_1.png.description: A tabular summary of the 20 “established” open-source Java projects (those created before Java generics) showing columns: Project name, number of developers (Devs), project age in years (Age), repository start and end dates (Start, End), and snapshot lines of code (LOC). The projects span start dates from 1998–2004 and end-date snapshots mostly in 2009–2010; developer counts range from 4 (FreeMind) up to 94 (JEdit) and ages from 3 to 11 years. Code size varies widely — examples include Xerces at 21,520 LOC on the small end and Hibernate at 3,125,097 LOC on the large end, with several mid-sized projects such as Commons Collections (235,487 LOC) and Eclipse-cs (592,214 LOC). These 20 projects comprise the “established” dataset used in the paper’s analysis (the authors state they mined full revision histories of these projects as part of their study).

page23_img_1.png.title: Raw vs. parameterized type usage over time in three projects
page23_img_1.png.description: Three time-series plots compare raw types (solid red) and parameterized types (dashed blue) with Date on the x‑axis and Number of Type Uses on the y‑axis. (a) Squirrel‑SQL: raw types grow from ~2002 to ~2006 (peak ≈1,000) then abruptly drop in mid‑2007 while parameterized types surge thereafter to ~2,500, indicating a concentrated migration event. (b) JEdit: raw types steadily increase to a large steady level (≈2,000–2,500) through 2006–2008 while parameterized uses rise later and eventually exceed raw uses by ~2010 (≈4,000), showing gradual adoption with many legacy raw uses remaining. (c) MiGen: a project started after generics, shows almost no raw types and a rapid increase in parameterized types from 2008 onward to over 10,000, illustrating that recent projects begin with and heavily favor generics.

page37_img_1.png.title: Contributor-level raw vs. generic type introductions/removals across established projects
page37_img_1.png.description: Grid of 20 small time-series plots (one per established project) showing developers’ introductions/removals of raw types (solid lines) and parameterized/generic types (dashed lines) over calendar time. Each colored pair of lines in a plot represents one of the five most active contributors (same color = same contributor), the x-axis is Date and the y-axis is labeled “Type Introductions/Removals” (note scales vary by project). The charts illustrate the paper’s finding that most projects exhibit one or two “champions” who add the majority of generics (e.g., Squirrel‑SQL shows a large jump in parameterized types in 2007), while a few projects (for example JEdit) show multiple contributors adopting generics roughly simultaneously; several plots also show abrupt bursts or large single-commit changes and widely different magnitudes (some projects reach thousands on the y-scale, others remain small).

page25_img_1.png.title: Contributors' raw vs. generic type introductions/removals (Squirrel‑SQL, JEdit, MiGen)
page25_img_1.png.description: Three time-series panels (x-axis = Date, y-axis = Type Introductions/Removals) plot the five most active contributors in each project; solid lines show raw-type uses and dashed lines show parameterized (generic) uses, with each color representing a different contributor. In Squirrel‑SQL (left) one contributor shows a sharp rise in parameterized types around 2007 while their raw-type count falls, indicating a concentrated migration effort. JEdit (center) shows several contributors beginning to add generics at about the same time (late 2006 onward), though contributors differ in magnitude of additions and removals. MiGen (right) is dominated by a single contributor who adds large numbers of parameterized types (y up to ~7000), while other contributors make only minor changes — illustrating the paper’s finding that new language features are typically introduced by a small number of “champions.”

page33_img_1.png.title: Cast vs. parameterized-type density over time in 20 established Java projects
page33_img_1.png.description: A 4x5 grid of small time-series plots, one per established project (titles like ant, jedit, squirrel‑sql, lucene, etc.), with the x‑axis spanning ~1998–2012 and the y‑axis showing element density (0–0.06). In each plot the red line tracks cast density and the blue line tracks parameterized-type (generics) density; in most projects the red line is substantially higher and the blue line remains near zero until the mid‑2000s. Several projects (for example Squirrel‑SQL, JEdit, JUnit, Lucene and Commons Collections) show a clear pattern where the blue line rises after 2004–2007 while the red line declines, whereas many other projects show persistent cast density with little generics adoption. The panel illustrates the paper’s finding that generics adoption is variable across projects and often (but not universally) coincides with a reduction in casts.

page15_img_1.png.title: Stacked counts of annotations, generics, and raw types in 20 recent Java projects
page15_img_1.png.description: Stacked vertical bars show, for each of 20 ‘recent’ projects on the x‑axis, the counts (in thousands on the y‑axis) of annotations (green), parameterized types/generics (blue), and raw types (red). Most projects have taller blue segments than red, indicating that generics are used more often than raw (the paper notes only 2 of the 20 projects had more raw types than generics), and almost every project also uses annotations. OpenSSO is the extreme outlier with by far the largest total and a very large red (raw type) component; MiGen (migen) also shows substantial use of generics. Four projects have no raw types at all (FlowGame, Ice4j, ReligionSearch, and SCSReader), consistent with the authors’ observation that some recent projects started after generics and therefore used them from the start.

page28_img_1.png.title: Days between introduction of generics and annotations (established vs recent projects)
page28_img_1.png.description: Two horizontal box plots compare, for established and recent project groups, the number of days between the first use of generics and the first use of annotations (negative values mean annotations were introduced before generics). The x‑axis is marked at decade-style intervals spanning roughly −1,000 to +10,000 days; the established projects’ box is much wider and shifted toward positive values (median well above zero) while the recent projects’ box is compact and clustered near zero with one large negative outlier. This visual supports the paper’s reported summary: established projects tended to stagger adoption (average lag ≈ 296 days), whereas recent projects adopted both features nearly simultaneously (average lag ≈ 53 days) with far less variation.

page36_img_1.png.title: Raw vs. parameterized (generic) type usage over time in recent projects
page36_img_1.png.description: A 4×6 grid of small time-series plots, one per recent project, showing counts of raw types (solid red line) and parameterized types (dashed blue line) on the y-axis over time on the x-axis. Most panels (e.g., encuestame, migen, pathvisio, makagiga) show parameterized types growing steadily and dominating raw-type use, indicating rapid adoption of generics; other projects (e.g., opensso) are clear outliers where raw types remain far more numerous than generics. Several projects (ehcache, libgdx, red5) show mixed behavior with early spikes in raw types followed by later increases in parameterized types, illustrating that migration patterns vary widely between projects. Overall the figure supports the paper’s observation that recent projects generally adopt generics broadly but adoption timing and the extent of migration from raw types differ by project.

page26_img_1.png.title: Contributors' annotation introductions over time (JDT, libgdx, MiGen)
page26_img_1.png.description: Three time-series plots (one per project) showing each project’s five most active contributors and the cumulative number of annotation introductions/removals on the y-axis over time on the x-axis. In org.eclipse.jdt (left) almost all annotation activity is from the contributor “oliviert” (purple), rising to ≈250 while the other four contributors remain near zero. In libgdx (center) the contributor “badlogicgames” (red) shows a very large burst beginning in 2010 up to ≈5,500 annotations and “nathan.sweet” (orange) adds about ≈1,200–1,400, with the remaining contributors near zero. In MiGen (right) several contributors (notably “darren.pearce” red, “toontalk@…” orange, and later “mavrikis” blue) each add substantial annotations (peaks around 1,500–1,700), illustrating a more distributed adoption; the abrupt large jumps (especially in libgdx) are consistent with the paper’s observation of bursty, possibly tool-driven annotation introductions.

page41_img_1.png.title: Springer publisher logo
page41_img_1.png.description: A black-and-white Springer publisher mark on a white background: the serif word “Springer” appears to the right of a small stylized knight/horse-head emblem (with a short horizontal rule beneath the icon). The image functions as the publisher imprint used in the paper (appearing near the end of the document, after the references) and identifies Springer Science+Business Media as the publisher.

page20_img_1.png.title: Cast vs. parameterized-type density over time for three projects
page20_img_1.png.description: Three time-series plots (years 2000–2011 on the x‑axis) compare cast density (red lines, top) with parameterized‑type density (blue lines, bottom) for Squirrel‑SQL, JEdit, and MiGen. The y‑axis shows density (program elements per unit Halstead program length); note the blue parameterized‑type series is plotted multiplied by 10 to make it visible. Squirrel‑SQL shows a clear rise in parameterized types beginning in 2007 accompanied by a concurrent drop in cast density (cast density falls from ~0.012 to ~0.007 while scaled parameterized density rises to ≈0.006–0.007 on the plot). JEdit shows parameterized types increasing from about 2005 with a gradual decline in casts (casts fall from a peak near 0.025 down toward ~0.01 by 2011), and MiGen exhibits a steep introduction of parameterized types around 2007 (scaled blue values rising to ~0.03–0.04) with a modest decline in cast density over the same period—patterns the paper cites as evidence that increased generics often correspond to reduced casts.

page35_img_1.png.title: Raw vs. parameterized type usage over time in established projects
page35_img_1.png.description: A 4x5 grid of small time-series plots (one per established project) showing number of type uses (y-axis) over time (x-axis). In each plot the solid red line is raw types (e.g., List) and the dashed blue line is parameterized types (generics); axes are labeled "Date" and "Number of Type Uses" and a legend appears in each pane. The panels illustrate heterogeneous adoption: many projects show raw types dominating for years with only small or late increases in generics (e.g., Jetty, Freemind), some show abrupt migrations where raw types drop while parameterized types rise (Squirrel‑SQL’s mid‑2007 shift corresponds to the paper’s reported conversion of 574 of 1411 raw types), and a few projects show strong early generic use (FindBugs and JEdit show large blue curves). Overall the figure visually supports the paper’s finding that full-scale migration from raw to parameterized types was uncommon and concentrated in a few projects.

page34_img_1.png.title: Casts vs. parameterized-type density over time in recent projects
page34_img_1.png.description: A 4×5 grid of small time-series plots, one per recent project (labels such as bbssh, ehcache, encuestame, flowgame, hummingbird, ice4j, libgdx, makagiga, migen, mobac, opensso, pathvisio, posterita, red5, religion-search, scsreader, smslib, vietocr, xbup, zkdesktop). Each plot shows years on the x‑axis (~2005–2011) and density on the y‑axis (0.00–0.06); red lines are cast density and blue lines are parameterized-type density (the paper notes the blue series is scaled by a factor of 10 for readability). The panels illustrate heterogeneous behavior across projects: some projects (e.g., migen, pathvisio) show a clear increase in parameterized-type density concurrent with a decline in casts, while others (e.g., hummingbird) show cast spikes without corresponding growth in generics, and several projects show both series rising or remaining flat. Overall the small multiples emphasize the paper’s point that the relationship between generics adoption and cast usage varies substantially across recent projects.

page38_img_1.png.title: Contributors' raw and parameterized type introductions over time (recent projects)
page38_img_1.png.description: A grid of small time-series plots (one panel per recent project) showing, for the five most active contributors, how many raw types (solid lines) and parameterized/generic types (dashed lines) each contributor introduced or removed over time. X-axes are Date and Y-axes are labeled “Type Introductions/Removals”; each color corresponds to a different contributor and a small legend in each panel marks solid=Raw and dashed=Generic. The panels reveal common patterns: many projects have one or two colored traces that dominate activity (sharp rises or large plateaus), while other contributors show little or intermittent use; some projects display abrupt bursts of many introductions in short time spans. This visual evidence supports the paper’s finding that adoption of generics in recent projects is typically driven by a small number of “champion” contributors rather than broad, simultaneous uptake by the community.

page42_img_1.png.title: Head-and-shoulders author portrait (man wearing glasses)
page42_img_1.png.description: Color photograph used in the paper’s author biographies showing a head-and-shoulders view of a man (unnamed). He wears rectangular eyeglasses, has short tousled hair, and rests his chin on his right fist with a slight, thoughtful smile. He is dressed in a dark jacket over a collared shirt; the background is an indoor, softly out-of-focus setting with vertical wooden panels and indistinct objects.

page43_img_1.png.title: Author head-and-shoulders portrait with glasses on red background
page43_img_1.png.description: A color head-and-shoulders portrait photograph used in the paper’s author biographies (page 43). The subject is an adult wearing dark rectangular eyeglasses and a black polo shirt, with short hair and a slight smile, photographed against a solid red backdrop that contains a faint numeric or patterned motif. The image is tightly framed around the face and upper torso with even, warm lighting and a neutral, professional expression.

page40_img_1.png.title: Per-contributor annotation introduction/removal time series for 20 recent Java projects
page40_img_1.png.description: The figure is a 4×5 grid of small time-series plots (one panel per project) showing annotation introductions and removals over time for 20 recent Java projects. Each panel has Date on the x‑axis and “Annotations Introductions/Removals” on the y‑axis, with color‑coded lines and a legend identifying the top contributors (by username or email); upward steps indicate annotation additions and downward steps indicate removals. Many panels show a single dominant contributor (red lines in panels such as encuestame, makagiga, and xbup) responsible for large, often abrupt increases, while others (e.g., flowgame, libgdx, red5, migen) show multiple contributors adding annotations; several panels exhibit very large spikes consistent with bulk or automated insertion. The plots visually support the paper’s observation that annotation usage is frequently driven by one or a few “champions,” with occasional short bursts of massive annotation additions and some small removal events.

page11_img_1.png.title: Table of 20 recent Java projects: devs, age, dates, and LOC
page11_img_1.png.description: This table lists 20 open-source Java projects that began after Java generics (columns: Project name, Devs, Age, Start, End, LOC). It reports team size (1–97 developers), project age (mostly 1–5 years), start and end snapshot dates, and source size in lines of code (LOC). Project sizes span from 3,858 LOC (SCSReader) up to 253,187 LOC (Makagiga), and the largest team is OpenSSO with 97 developers (241,062 LOC); several projects are single‑developer efforts (e.g., BBSSH, Makagiga, VietOCR, XBUP). Most projects’ end dates in the table are in 2011, with a few earlier terminations (e.g., Zero Kelvin Desktop ended 12/12/2008, Posterita ended 3/31/2009, OpenSSO ended 3/4/2010).

page42_img_2.png.title: Smiling head-and-shoulders portrait of a man in a striped shirt
page42_img_2.png.description: Color head-and-shoulders photograph of a smiling adult man with short dark hair, shown slightly turned to his left. He wears a light-colored collared shirt with thin horizontal stripes; the image is tightly cropped to the face and upper shoulders and lit evenly, producing a mild forehead highlight. The background shows diagonal dark and light bands; the photo appears among the paper’s author portraits, but I cannot identify the individual by name.
